The STREAM Group aims to accelerate the development of current and future energy-related technologies by providing an atomistic-level understanding of key processes occurring at liquid–solid interfaces.

Our research is organised around three connected threads. We study **aqueous and electrified interfaces**, where a few molecular layers of water in contact with an electrode govern the performance of batteries, fuel cells and electrolysers, and where the role of interfacial water structure is still far from established. We investigate **nuclear quantum dynamics**, because the light hydrogen nucleus keeps its quantum character at room temperature and zero-point energy and tunnelling can change reaction rates by orders of magnitude. And we develop the theory of **nonlinear vibrational spectroscopy**, computing surface-specific observables such as sum-frequency generation and tip-enhanced Raman spectra from first principles, which gives us a direct, quantitative link to experiment.

To tackle these questions we combine a hierarchy of simulation methods, from classical force fields through ab initio density functional theory to machine-learning potentials, with path-integral techniques that treat the nuclei quantum mechanically in systems of thousands of atoms. Much of this work goes into open community codes such as i-PI and FHI-aims.

We enjoy collaborating with experimentalists and theoreticians alike to address challenging problems in interfacial chemistry, electrochemistry, spectroscopy, and energy-related materials.
